name: Financial Times cryptic crossword, Penguin book 1 No 6

book.title: The Penguin Book of Financial Times Crosswords, volume 1

clue.text: Sit and rob a mixture from the wine shop

indicators.note: a mixture is several things stirred together, so the preceding words are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sits down in a wine bar and mugs a customer, a crime scene stirred up in a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sit and rob' reads like two actions, but the words are only raw letters for shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: A bistro is a small, informal restaurant or bar where wine is served with simple food.

clue.text: City gent saves his bacon

blocks.note: first meaning: a fellow from the city of Bath
second meaning: a cured cut of pork

explanation.surface: A businessman from London's financial district escapes disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City gent' suggests a stockbroker in the City of London; read it as a chap from Bath. 'Saves his' joins them, with cured meat being saved bacon. A Bath chap is the cured lower cheek of a pig.
explanation.definitionFit: This West Country speciality is pig's cheek that has been salted and smoked, a traditional cured pork product.

clue.text: The answer is a patron of seamen or possibly it's a lemon

definitions.text: The answer is a patron of seamen

indicators.note: possibly means the words could be read another way, so the letters may be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A puzzled solver guesses whether the answer is a sailors' saint or just a dud.
explanation.walkthrough: A lemon is British slang for a dud, so the surface offers the answer as either a saint or a failure.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Erasmus, known as Elmo, is the patron of sailors, who named the electrical glow on masts after him.

clue.text: A short prayer makes the oriental mellow

blocks.note: RIP abbreviates the prayer requiescat in pace, rest in peace
E is the abbreviation for east, the Orient

explanation.surface: A brief prayer softens an Eastern visitor's mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripe and mellow both describe fruit or wine that has fully matured and become soft and full-flavoured.

clue.text: Sacred measure in the Palace

blocks.note: sacred and holy are synonyms
a rood is an old measure of land, a quarter of an acre

explanation.surface: A religious ceremony of measuring something within a royal residence.
explanation.walkthrough: A rood is also a cross, which keeps the surface churchy. Holyroodhouse in Edinburgh is the monarch's official residence in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Holyrood is the familiar short name for the royal palace of Holyroodhouse at the foot of Edinburgh's Royal Mile.

clue.text: Matricide chased by the Furies

blocks.note: surface reading: a mother-killer hounded by avenging spirits
setter's reading: the son of Agamemnon in Greek tragedy who killed Clytemnestra

explanation.walkthrough: In Aeschylus's Oresteia the hero avenges his father by killing his mother and is pursued by the Erinyes until Athena acquits him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek legend's prince slew his mother Clytemnestra and was then hounded by avenging goddesses, as told in Aeschylus.

clue.text: 'Myself with — Seven thousand years' (Omar)

blocks.note: surface reading: a line of verse with a gap
setter's reading: fill the gap from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam

explanation.walkthrough: The Rubaiyat line runs 'Tomorrow! — Why, Tomorrow I may be / Myself with Yesterday's Sev'n Thousand Years'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in FitzGerald's famous translated quatrain is the possessive of the day before today, referring to all past time.

clue.text: Look up, I've got the girl

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: lo is an old word for look or behold
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone tells a friend to look, because they've landed a girlfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look up' sounds like consulting a reference; 'up' only turns the short word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive is a girl's given name; crosswords often define a forename this way, as a girl or woman.

clue.text: The fellow had a meal to give

blocks.note: a don is a fellow of a university college
having a meal means eating, past tense

explanation.surface: A man was served dinner in order to make a contribution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' looks like any man, but a university fellow is a don.
explanation.definitionFit: To donate is to give money or goods as a gift, typically to a charity or cause.

clue.text: Saw the way he bled

indicators.note: the way something happened is its manner or arrangement, so the next words are put in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A witness watched how a wounded man bled, or a saw cut him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' tempts as the cutting tool; it is the past tense of see.
explanation.definitionFit: Beheld is the past tense of behold, an older word for looking at or seeing something.

clue.text: Late epic I turn into a postscript

indicators.note: to turn something into something else is to transform it, so these letters are remade in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet decides to convert a late long poem into an afterword.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailpiece is a part added at the end of a book or piece of writing, much as an appended note follows a letter.

clue.text: Graft — the colonel is mixed up with the offence

indicators.note: being mixed up with something means being jumbled together, so both pieces are combined and rearranged

blocks.note: CO is the commanding officer, here the colonel
a sin is a moral offence

explanation.surface: An officer is implicated in a corruption scandal, with graft meaning bribery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Graft' looks like corruption to suit the colonel's offence, but it is the gardener's sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In horticulture a scion is a cut shoot attached to a rootstock, which is exactly what a gardener's graft is.

clue.text: He insisted on the destruction of Carthage

definitions.text: He insisted on the destruction of Carthage

blocks.clueFragment: He insisted on the destruction of Carthage
blocks.note: surface reading: a description of some ancient warmonger

blocks.clueFragment: He insisted on the destruction of Carthage
blocks.note: setter's reading: the Roman senator who ended every speech demanding that Carthage be destroyed

explanation.walkthrough: Cato the Elder famously closed his speeches with 'Carthago delenda est', Carthage must be destroyed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman statesman Marcus Porcius Cato repeatedly urged the Senate to wipe out its African rival before the Third Punic War.

clue.text: Reckoning in the colony

blocks.note: first meaning: the paying or squaring up of an account
second meaning: a community founded by people moving to a new land

explanation.surface: Accounts are being totted up somewhere in a colonial outpost.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both the final paying off of a debt and a place where newcomers have established a community.

clue.text: Loses control like an old car

definitions.note: describes what an old car does: stops working

blocks.note: first meaning: gives way to emotion and collapses in tears
second meaning: stops working mechanically, as an aged vehicle does

explanation.surface: A driver loses control just as an ancient car tends to.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both an emotional collapse into tears and a machine failing and ceasing to run.

clue.text: Tempted by all the colour round you

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: taken as written
red stands as the archetypal colour
U is the text-speak spelling of you

explanation.surface: Someone is lured on by bright colours surrounding them on every side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round you' reads as the colour encircling a person; it means the colour's letters encircle the text-speak letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To be allured is to be enticed or attracted by something, the same as being tempted.

clue.text: Ecclesiastic in the auction gets the joint

indicators.note: one piece placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: an auction is a kind of sale
DD is Doctor of Divinity, a churchman's degree

explanation.surface: A clergyman at an auction successfully bids for a cut of meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a hip or knee, or a dive, but here it is a butcher's cut.
explanation.definitionFit: A saddle of lamb or mutton is a butcher's cut taken from both loins, a classic roasting joint of meat.

clue.text: Animal courage distinguishes the English king

blocks.note: the lion is an animal
heart means courage, as in take heart

explanation.surface: Bold animal bravery marks out a monarch of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard I of England was nicknamed Coeur de Lion, the Lionheart.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard the First earned the nickname for his bravery on crusade, so the epithet names that medieval monarch.

clue.text: Crimes of receivers

blocks.note: taken as written
a fence is a receiver of stolen goods

explanation.surface: Charges brought against people who handle stolen property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Receivers' sounds like radio sets or accountants; in crime slang they are dealers in stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Offences are breaches of the law, illegal acts punishable by the courts, which is what crimes are.

clue.text: Polish in Hamlet

blocks.note: surface reading: shining up a small village
setter's reading: the word Shakespeare's play uses for a native of Poland

explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like the verb to shine and 'Hamlet' like a little village; the capitals hide a Pole as named in the play, where Old Hamlet 'smote the sledded Polacks on the ice'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy uses this archaic word to mean a Pole, so it is how Polish people are named there.

clue.text: A spoil-sport — but why murder the girl?

blocks.note: to murder is to kill
Joy is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone spoils the fun, yet one asks why anyone would murder a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A killjoy deliberately dampens others' enjoyment, the same kind of person as a spoil-sport.

clue.text: Raise a false alarm

blocks.note: surface reading: set off an alarm when there is no danger
setter's reading: the idiom from Aesop's fable of the shepherd boy who shouted about a predator

explanation.walkthrough: In Aesop's fable the shepherd boy calls out falsely so often that nobody believes him when the danger is real.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from a fable about a shepherd boy and means to summon help needlessly, giving unfounded warnings.

clue.text: One can find another for the dance

blocks.note: a single tin
a second tin of the same kind

explanation.surface: A person can find a partner for the dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One can' reads as 'a person is able to'; it is one tin, followed by another.
explanation.definitionFit: The cancan is a high-kicking dance of the Paris music halls, associated with the Moulin Rouge.

clue.text: With temporary authority on the stage

blocks.note: first meaning: serving as a stand-in, like a temporary chairman
second meaning: performing as a player in the theatre

explanation.surface: Someone is briefly in charge of a theatre performance.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means holding an office temporarily for someone else and also performing roles in plays as a profession.

clue.text: Turns up to rehabilitate the Mongol case

indicators.note: rehabilitating something rebuilds it into a new state, so the letters are reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written, without the article

explanation.surface: Someone arrives to reform a convicted Mongol or reopen his legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the letters of 'Mongol case' are rearranged; 'the' is part of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: When someone arrives or appears unexpectedly they turn up; the phrasal verb means much the same as arrive.

clue.text: Grain for one in bewilderment

indicators.note: one piece placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: to be in a maze is to be bewildered or confused
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone is confused about cereals, as though asking which grain is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For one' looks like 'for example'; 'for' only links, and 'one' is the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Maize is a cereal crop, also called corn in North America, grown for its edible kernels.

clue.text: It's a drag when she's about, love

indicators.note: being about something means surrounding it, so one piece is placed around another

blocks.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A grumble that it is tedious when a certain woman is hanging around, darling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a drag' reads as a complaint about boredom, but a drag is a brake.
explanation.definitionFit: A drag shoe, or skid, is a brake block pressed against a wheel to slow a cart or carriage downhill.

clue.text: A type of china to steal

blocks.note: first meaning: fine porcelain made with ash from animal skeletons
second meaning: old slang verb for pilfering

explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is also rhyming slang for mate, but here it is porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: Bone china is a translucent porcelain, and as dated slang the verb also means pinching or making off with something.

clue.text: Mr Jones announces his entry

blocks.note: surface reading: a man named Jones, perhaps a butler's caller being shown in
setter's reading: the words a man says as he steps in, run together, make the first name of a famous Jones

explanation.surface: A man called Jones declares his arrival as he walks in.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken on entering, 'in I go' runs together into the name. The Mr Jones meant is Inigo Jones, the seventeenth-century English architect of the Banqueting House in Whitehall.
explanation.definitionFit: Inigo Jones was the famous English architect and stage designer, so this first name identifies that particular gentleman.

clue.text: Leader of the French resistance

blocks.note: surface reading: a commander of the wartime Résistance against occupation
setter's reading: the medieval peasant girl who led France against the English in the Hundred Years War

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase makes us think of the 1940s underground; the setter means the fifteenth-century resistance to English invaders.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maid of Orléans led French forces to raise the siege of Orléans in 1429, rallying her nation against English occupation.

clue.text: Jealousy in an inexperienced detective

blocks.note: green means new to something, untrained
a private eye is a detective

explanation.surface: A rookie investigator is consumed by envy of colleagues.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare calls envy the green-eyed monster, so the green eye is a traditional emblem standing for envious feelings.

clue.text: Happy events, we hear, on board

definitions.note: a phrase describing where the answer is found: places to sleep on board ship

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken aloud, so the sound matters and not the spelling

blocks.note: a happy event is a euphemism for a baby being born

explanation.surface: Babies are being born aboard a ship, it is rumoured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happy event' is an old-fashioned euphemism for the arrival of a baby.
explanation.definitionFit: Berths are the bunks or sleeping places provided for passengers and crew aboard a ship or train.
